9/12/2026, 12:24:40 AM

What was actually new from this pass is much narrower:

New evidence, not a new solution

Kepler gives a direct search instruction to Fludd

In the 1622 first-edition Apologia, printed p. 41, Kepler challenges Fludd:

Age namque dic ubi tu semitonium colloces…

Essentially: “Come then, say where you place the semitone.”

This may be the explicit pointer you suspected their debate would contain. It directs the reader back into Fludd’s diagrams to locate the semitone. Whether you already had this passage determines whether it is genuinely new.

Kepler identifies Fludd’s precise theoretical error

On printed p. 14, Kepler says Fludd confused:

Plato/Pythagorean limma 256:243, and

Ptolemaic/just semitone 16:15.

That makes the comma correction an intentional subject of their dispute, not merely a relationship recoverable from modern interval arithmetic.

Fludd answers the “where?” question spatially

In the 1622 first-edition Monochordum Mundi:

printed p. 54 places the limma specifically in the E–F space;

printed pp. 78–80 answers Ad Analysin XXV by locating the semitone where light predominates: Fire, the Sun, the stellar heaven and the Seraphic region.

That gives two different meanings of “where”:

\text{musical location}=E\!-\!F

\text{cosmic location}=\text{Fire/Sun/stars/Seraphim}.

The conjunction may be important: Kepler asks where the semitone is; Fludd answers both on the monochord and in the cosmic hierarchy.

The octave landing is explicitly a separate Fludd operation

The following first-edition page gives the same-letter next-register construction by geometrical bisection. Therefore MI–FA–MI performs the excursion and return, while Fludd’s bisection performs the octave landing. This resolves an ambiguity in the boundary equation, but may already be part of your newer work.

Corrections and exclusions

The “same publisher” hypothesis is presently false as stated

The verified imprints do not show one shared publisher:

Fludd/Otreb: de Bry–Galler network.

Kepler’s 1619 Harmonices: Tampach/Planck.

Kepler’s 1622 Apologia: Tampach.

Fludd’s 1622 Monochordum: de Bry.

There may be a shared Frankfurt printer, engraver, compositor or distribution network, but that remains unproved.

Otreb’s marginal “Ex Fama” is not a famine clue

It refers to material taken from the Rosicrucian Fama. It does not independently point to Kepler’s famem. Otreb still supplies Earth, misery, bread, planetary pipes and cyclical restoration—but not the comma.

Unresolved leads—not findings

The strongest untested leads are:

Temple of Music, printed p. 161
 Your scan combines solmization syllables with a numerical apparatus containing 81. It might cross-point MI–FA and the comma, but I have not established the reading.

World Monochord’s F/F♯ discrepancy
 Modern scholarship claims both F positions must effectively be sharpened for the engraved tones and semitones to work. This must be checked directly against the 1617 plate and surrounding Latin.

Fludd’s reply to Analysis XXV
 The complete pp. 78–80 response needs to be mapped symbol-by-symbol back onto the 1617 engravings. That is the likeliest textual-to-visual pointer currently visible.

Diagrammatic “Fludd comma” versus 81:80
 Your measured approximately 21.5-cent plate anomaly must not automatically be identified with Kepler’s 81:80. Their relationship remains unproved.

So the honest accounting is:

New hidden correspondence discovered: none yet.

Potentially new primary textual pointer: Kepler’s “where do you place the semitone?”

Newly verified response location: Fludd’s Ad Analysin XXV, pp. 78–80.

New elimination: no demonstrated common publisher.

Best remaining graphical target: the p. 161 Temple-of-Music numerical/solmization grid.

The hour produced source verification and narrowed targets, but it did not yet produce the kind of new concealed correspondence you requested.
